subtopics.title: Carbon allotropes and property differences

slots.X: Two ideal carbon network fragments have 12 carbon atoms each with periodic boundaries. Model A has four neighbours per carbon; B has three in-plane neighbours per carbon. Draw the local arrangements, count distinct nearest-neighbour links in each model and connect the diagrams to direction-dependent transport without treating link count as bond strength.
slots.Y: Coordination is the number of nearest bonded neighbours, not bond order or isolated bond strength. In an ideal periodic network each link is shared by two atoms; graphite has delocalised electrons in layers.
slots.Z: A tetrahedral 3D network, B trigonal planar in sheets. Each link counted twice: A=24, B=18. B has delocalised electrons in layers, A normally lacks mobile carriers. Link count is topology, not bond energy or conductivity magnitude. Periodic boundary idealisation avoids edge effects.
slots.W: Translate coordination into local geometry, network link counts and transport interpretation.

subtopics.title: Saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons

slots.X: A neutral connected hydrocarbon C₅H₈ is claimed to contain exactly one C=C, no rings and no other multiple bonds. Test claim by valence counting and construct two valid structures with different ring/multiple-bond allocations; verify both formulas.
slots.Y: For typical neutral connected hydrocarbons, a ring or double bond reduces hydrogen count by two relative to acyclic saturation; triple reduces by four. Hydrogen-deficiency formula is extension context; formula alone does not identify structure.
slots.Z: C₅H₁₂ saturated acyclic; missing 4 H corresponds to two unsaturation units. One double gives C₅H₁₀. Pent-1-yne HC≡C–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ has 8 H; cyclopentene has one ring and one double, two CH and three CH₂=8 H. Formula cannot determine connectivity.
slots.W: Build two valid structures and reject incompatible hydrogen count.

slots.Y: Hydrogen deficiency counts rings and multiple bonds; ideal hydrogenation consumes one H₂ per C=C and two per C≡C. Ring preservation is an explicit condition. Extension counting model, not a procedure.
slots.Z: C₄H₆ has two deficiency units relative to C₄H₁₀. Two H₂ add four H; final acyclic so initial no ring under model. But-1-yne HC≡C–CH₂–CH₃ and buta-1,3-diene CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ both meet total uptake and yield butane. Distinguish via suitable structural spectroscopy or bond-specific evidence. Hydrogen uptake alone does not choose triple vs two doubles.
slots.W: Combine formula and selective reaction constraints; construct distinct compatible structures.

subtopics.title: Ethanol, ethanoic acid, soaps and detergents

slots.X: Two ideal surfactant sketches show (A) heads at the water-facing surface and tails toward an oil droplet, (B) heads buried in oil and tails facing water. Represent both with labelled water/oil regions and explain which orientation supports an oil-in-water dispersion. Predict what changes when calcium binds the soap heads.
slots.Y: Amphiphilic molecules contain hydrophobic tails and hydrophilic heads; aggregate geometry depends on surrounding phases. Divalent ions can remove soap through precipitation, distinct from micellisation.
slots.Z: A is compatible with aqueous dispersion: hydrophobic tails associate with oil, ionic hydrophilic heads contact water. B reversed orientation is not typical oil-in-water arrangement. Ca²⁺ can form sparingly soluble carboxylate salt, reducing available active soap; not every remaining aggregate behaves identically. Foam not a direct measure of removal.
slots.W: Construct labelled molecular orientation and connect changed head chemistry to dispersion.

slots.X: A hypothetical soap contains 0.012 mol RCOO⁻. Water contains 0.003 mol Ca²⁺ and 0.001 mol Mg²⁺; both precipitate quantitatively as (RCOO)₂M. Calculate lost and remaining soap, compare 0.004 mol Na⁺ alone, and explain why remaining amount does not uniquely predict foam height; propose detergent control.
slots.Y: Soap has ionic carboxylate heads and hydrophobic tails. Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ can form sparingly soluble salts, removing active soap. Synthetic detergent response depends on formulation. Distinguish precipitation, micelles and foam measurements.
slots.Z: Divalent ions consume 2(0.003+0.001)=0.008 mol carboxylate; 0.004 remains. Na⁺ does not form analogous insoluble divalent salt in model, though ionic strength can change solubility. Foam depends on formulation, concentration, agitation and temperature; compare equal active concentrations, volumes, hardness. Detergents are not universally immune.
slots.W: Combine ion stoichiometry, competing salt effects and fair experimental comparison.

slots.X: Two pure liquids are ethanol and ethanoic acid. In ideal separate tests an equal 0.050 mol portion of each is contacted with excess hydrogen carbonate; one generates 0.050 mol CO₂ and the other none. Equal portions are then combined in a theoretical 1:1 esterification with 60% conversion. Justify identification, calculate ester/water and remaining reactants, and explain why the initial gas observation does not establish a real mixture's purity.
slots.Y: Carboxylic acid can transfer proton to hydrogen carbonate. Esterification is reversible; conversion controls product amount. Distinguish functional-group evidence from purity and theoretical yield.
slots.Z: Acid + HCO₃⁻→CH₃COO⁻+CO₂+H₂O; ethanoic acid gives .050 mol CO₂, ethanol no analogous response. CH₃COOH+C₂H₅OH⇌CH₃COOC₂H₅+H₂O. .030 mol ester and water; .020 mol acid and ethanol remain. Gas identifies acidic behaviour within pure candidates, not arbitrary mixtures. Separate portions, no practical instructions.
slots.W: Justify identification and cross-check reaction amounts under stated conversion and purity assumptions.
